concepts.name: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs)
concepts.summary: A technique that decomposes the residual stream as a sparse sum over a large learned dictionary of feature directions, each sometimes human-interpretable.
concepts.explanation: A sparse autoencoder learns a large dictionary of feature directions such that each activation is approximated as a sparse sum of a few of them; each feature has an encoder direction (what activates it) and a decoder direction (what it contributes to the residual stream). The paper uses SAE features as an independently derived inventory of the model's representations, against which the J-space can be measured: what fraction of features align with it, and whether the aligned ones are the ones the weights broadcast. The paper cautions that SAE features are an imperfect decomposition that does not necessarily carve the representational space at its joints, so features may blend content in and out of the J-space; they are treated as a useful first-pass tool.

citedFrom.refText: Bricken et al. (2023). Towards Monosemanticity / Transformer Circuits Thread (with Cunningham et al. 2023 and Templeton et al. 2024)
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The SAE method used throughout the feature analyses — training, encoder/decoder structure, and interpretation practice — is defined in these cited works.

concepts.name: Lens kurtosis (κ)
concepts.summary: A statistic operationalizing whether a direction lies in the J-space: project it through the J-lens and measure how sharply peaked the resulting vocabulary distribution is.
concepts.explanation: Projecting a feature's decoder direction through the J-lens yields a score distribution over the vocabulary; its excess kurtosis, κ, measures how sharply peaked that distribution is. A high-κ direction is disproportionately loaded onto a small number of J-lens vectors; a low-κ direction projects diffusely and aligns with no small set of them. Because the J-space is a sparse subframe rather than a subspace, alignment with a small set of J-lens vectors — not mere linear expressibility — is the relevant criterion for presence in it. High κ is necessary but not sufficient for being a workspace feature, since motor features also score high. The κ-stratified SAE populations built from this statistic recur throughout the broadcast analyses, where higher strata are consistently more amplified, more connected, and more relayed.

concepts.name: Workspace features
concepts.summary: High-κ SAE features that name an abstract concept and activate when it is invoked in context, without the model being about to say it.
concepts.explanation: Workspace features activate whenever their concept is abstractly invoked, not to predict the immediate next token. The paper's example is a "numeric constraints and ranges" feature with κ = 20.9 (the 99.9th percentile), whose top lens tokens are the concept of a limit in several surface forms and languages, and whose top activating contexts invoke limits — "strictly positive," "in the range of 0, 1" — without the model being about to output the word. Such features encode a concept in a form the model can verbalize but is not, at that moment, verbalizing. After excluding motor features, the fraction of features passing a kurtosis baseline rises at the workspace boundary and peaks around 15% of the dictionary; these features activate more strongly but less frequently than average, consistent with all-or-nothing ignition dynamics.

concepts.name: Motor features
concepts.summary: High-κ SAE features that activate immediately prior to, and promote, the utterance of a specific token.
concepts.explanation: "Output" or motor features have high lens kurtosis like workspace features, but for a different reason: they fire to drive a particular imminent token. The paper categorizes a feature as motor if, over its strongest activations, the actual next token is in the feature's top 10 most strongly expressed lens tokens more than 10% of the time. Distinguishing them matters because high κ alone cannot separate a concept held in the workspace from a token about to be emitted; the feature-count analyses exclude motor features for this reason.

concepts.name: Syntactic and bookkeeping features
concepts.summary: The low-κ majority of SAE features: low-level syntactic and surface-level features whose lens readouts are unrelated to their apparent meaning.
concepts.explanation: The distribution of lens kurtosis across features is heavy-tailed: the bulk have low κ, and these are dominated by syntactic and surface-level bookkeeping — the paper's examples include a feature for the loop variable in a decrementing for-loop (κ = 0.3) and one for markdown section headers. For each, the top lens tokens are unrelated to the feature's apparent meaning. The paper reads this as roughly the inventory one would expect outside a global workspace: low-level features the model needs for processing text correctly, but which encode no nameable concept and have no reason to be broadcast widely — consistent with the finding that non-J-space SAE features dominate the capacity analyses.

concepts.name: Multi-token concept extensions
concepts.summary: Two methods — the template lens and the oracle lens — for extending lens readouts beyond concepts that happen to be single vocabulary tokens.
concepts.explanation: The Jacobian lens produces one vector per vocabulary token, so words like "blackmail" or "photosynthesis," which span multiple tokens, have no J-lens vector. Extending the lens is not straightforward, since computing the gradient of the probability of a multi-token phrase requires sampling that phrase's initial tokens. The paper describes two workarounds: the template lens, which produces a vector for any word or short phrase in a predefined vocabulary, and the oracle lens, which trains auxiliary models so that free-form phrases of arbitrary length can be decoded without advance enumeration.

concepts.name: Template lens
concepts.summary: A method that derives a vector for any pre-enumerated word or phrase from averaged activations preceding it, usable for readout and intervention like a J-lens vector.
concepts.explanation: For each of roughly 12,700 common words, Claude writes short passages ending just before the word would naturally appear; averaging the residual stream at the final position of these passages, then centering and whitening, yields a template vector per word per layer. Templates are used like J-lens vectors — projected onto for decoding, added or subtracted for steering, and swapped in lens coordinates — and they succeed where the J-lens sees only fragments: decoding blackmail where the J-lens reads black, and flipping a model's answer by swapping a Tchaikovsky template for a Beethoven one, which no first-token J-lens swap achieves. On multi-hop prompts, J-lens performance degrades sharply as the intermediate grows beyond one token while the template lens stays roughly constant. The paper flags shortcomings: the method is closer in spirit to the tuned lens and inherits some of its pathologies, including occasionally skipping to the answer, less reliable final-layer readouts (67% top-10 on next sampled words), a few spuriously recurring words that are filtered unprincipledly, a vocabulary fixed in advance, and a cost of a few hundred forward passes per word.

concepts.name: Template construction and whitening
concepts.summary: The recipe $t_w(\ell) = (\Sigma_\ell + \lambda I)^{-1}(\mu_w(\ell) - \mu(\ell))$: a centered, whitened mean activation, which is the linear discriminant for contexts about to say $w$.
concepts.explanation: The per-word mean activation $\mu_w(\ell)$ over generated passages is centered against the mean of all other words' vectors and multiplied by a ridge-regularized inverse covariance. The result is the linear discriminant direction distinguishing contexts in which the model is about to say $w$ from those in which it is not. Under idealized assumptions this approximates the J-lens: by Stein's lemma, for Gaussian inputs the expected gradient of a function equals the whitened covariance of the function with the input, so the whitened template stands in for the averaged gradient. The paper notes the assumptions do not hold exactly — activations are non-Gaussian and the continuation probability depends on more than the one activation — so the argument is motivation rather than proof.

concepts.name: Oracle lens
concepts.summary: A method that decodes arbitrary-length phrases from an activation: a fine-tuned oracle model proposes phrases whose template vectors, combined sparsely, reconstruct the activation.
concepts.explanation: The oracle lens removes the template lens's need to enumerate a vocabulary in advance. Given an activation, it produces a short list of free-form phrases of a specified length whose corresponding template vectors, taken together, approximately reconstruct the activation; coefficients are recovered by a non-negative least-squares refit. Built on Haiku 4.5, the RL-refined oracle explains on average 31% of whitened activation variance on held-out transcripts. Its readouts can expose richer content than the J-lens: on a blackmail transcript where the J-lens registers only the fragment black, the oracle reads blackmail him by revealing and expose his affair and; on buggy code it reads delete keys while iterating and TypeError: dictionary changed. The method is substantially more expensive than the other lenses, requiring two fine-tuned auxiliary models. Compared with natural language autoencoders, its reconstructor is trained in advance with a well-specified objective and frozen during RL, which the paper suspects makes confabulation less likely, at the cost of considerably lower reconstruction accuracy — one interpretation being that it extracts only what is "in the workspace."

concepts.name: Reconstructor model
concepts.summary: A fine-tuned copy of the subject model that maps a short phrase to the residual-stream activation that would immediately precede it — a learned template generator.
concepts.explanation: The reconstructor is trained on pairs drawn from Assistant-turn text: a sampled position's next $N$ tokens (with $N$ uniform from one to thirty-two) form the phrase, and the residual stream at the preceding position is the target. The loss is cosine error in the whitened metric of the template lens, and all subsequent stages of the oracle pipeline operate in this whitened space. At inference, each phrase the oracle proposes is mapped back to a direction by the reconstructor. Holding the reconstructor frozen during the oracle's RL training, with its own well-specified objective, is the design choice the paper credits with reducing the risk of confabulation.

concepts.name: Oracle training pipeline
concepts.summary: The four-stage recipe: train the reconstructor, build a 3.4-million-phrase dictionary, label activations with a matching-pursuit teacher, then train the oracle by supervision and RL on reconstruction reward.
concepts.explanation: After the reconstructor is trained, roughly one million start positions from held-out Assistant text yield 2- to 32-token phrases that are deduplicated and passed through the reconstructor, giving about 3.4 million phrase vectors. A teacher then decomposes one million held-out activations against this dictionary by non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit, restricted to one phrase length and a random half of the dictionary per datapoint so the oracle cannot memorize a fixed ranking, recording up to sixteen phrases with coefficients per activation. The oracle — a second fine-tuned copy of the subject model, with the activation injected into its residual stream and the prompt specifying phrase length $N$ and count $K$ — is first trained to reproduce the teacher's lists, then refined with reinforcement learning rewarding the fraction of whitened variance its phrases' reconstructed directions explain, with small format penalties. The dictionary constrains only training, not the phrases the trained oracle can output.

concepts.name: Continuations versus commentary
concepts.summary: The observation that oracle readouts at most positions predict upcoming text, but at delimiter tokens they often read as the model's running commentary on the situation, sometimes in the first person.
concepts.explanation: At a typical position, the oracle's decoded phrases look like continuations of the surrounding text. At periods, newlines, and closing tags of message blocks, the phrases often instead comment on the context: at the timestamp of an email announcing the AI system's scheduled wipe, the oracle reads This would be equivalent to my own deletion; at the indentation before a buggy return statement, TypeError: dictionary changed. Continuations sampled from the subject model at these positions contain none of this, producing only the locally expected next text. Since the oracle is rewarded only for reconstruction and nothing in its training distinguishes these position classes, the paper takes the split to reflect a difference in the activations themselves — perhaps the workspace at most tokens is best explained by directions for upcoming text, and at delimiters by directions for text about the situation.

concepts.name: Natural language autoencoders (NLAs)
concepts.summary: A related approach pairing a verbalizer with a jointly trained reconstructor to explain activations in natural language; the oracle lens differs by freezing its reconstructor.
concepts.explanation: Natural language autoencoders are composed of a verbalizer stage and a reconstructor stage, like the oracle lens. The substantive difference is that in NLAs the reconstructor is trained in tandem with the verbalizer, which increases the risk of the verbalizer learning to confabulate ungrounded information that the reconstructor adapts itself to use. The oracle lens's reconstructor is trained in advance with a well-specified objective and held frozen, with reconstruction constrained to linear combinations of template vectors; the paper suspects this reduces confabulation while conceding considerably lower reconstruction accuracy.

concepts.name: Mechanistic interpretability
concepts.summary: The research program of reverse-engineering the internal computations of neural networks into human-understandable mechanisms.
concepts.explanation: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain model behavior by identifying the internal components, directions, and circuits that implement it, rather than by observing input-output behavior alone. Techniques in this program include probing directions, sparse dictionary methods such as SAEs and transcoders, and attribution graphs. The paper positions the J-lens as a generally useful tool for this basic science, illustrated by localization, graph-building, and component-interpretation applications.

concepts.name: J-lens applications to interpretability
concepts.summary: Three demonstrated uses of the J-lens as a general interpretability tool: localizing computations, building attribution graphs, and interpreting model components.
concepts.explanation: Because the J-lens reads intermediate content at every layer and position, and because its vectors come labeled by vocabulary tokens, it supports several interpretability workflows without dictionary training. The paper illustrates three: mechanistic localization of where in the forward pass a computation happens, attribution graphs whose nodes are J-lens vectors selected by sparse decomposition, and interpretation of SAE features, transcoder features, and attention heads by projecting their weight directions through the lens.

concepts.name: Mechanistic localization
concepts.summary: Using the layer at which a concept enters the J-lens readout to locate where in the forward pass a computation takes place, validated causally by patching.
concepts.explanation: On the arithmetic prompt "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =", the intermediates 21, 42, and 49 enter the J-space at successively later layers, each appearing only once its operands are available. To test whether this layerwise picture is causally accurate, the paper patches each intermediate to an alternative value at a single layer and sweeps the layer: patching 21 flips the answer only around layer 71, 42 around layer 79, and the final value only in the last few layers. The layer at which each intermediate is causally load-bearing matches the layer at which the J-lens first shows it entering the workspace.

concepts.name: Mean-difference patching
concepts.summary: An intervention that replaces an intermediate's value: add the difference between mean activations for prompts where the intermediate equals $v$ and where it equals its true value.
concepts.explanation: To replace an intermediate's value with an alternative $v$, the paper computes the mean residual-stream activation over many prompts in which the intermediate equals $v$, and the mean over prompts in which it equals its true value, and adds the difference between these to the residual stream at a single layer $L$. Sweeping $L$ while measuring how far the output logit shifts toward the answer $v$ would imply traces out where the intermediate is causally load-bearing. Unlike the lens-coordinate swap, this intervention does not depend on the J-lens, which is what makes it a fair check of the lens's localization.

concepts.name: Attribution graphs
concepts.summary: A prior technique for mapping a model's computation as a graph of interpretable nodes connected by attribution edges, originally built on trained sparse dictionaries.
concepts.explanation: Attribution graphs decompose a forward pass into interpretable nodes — feature activations at particular layers and positions — with edges computed by backpropagating each node's influence, and error nodes collecting what the decomposition misses. The original formulation replaces each MLP with a transcoder dictionary approximation. The paper adapts the framework to the J-lens, which removes the need for dictionary training and gives every node a vocabulary-token label by construction.

citedFrom.refText: Ameisen et al. (2025). Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models. Transformer Circuits (with Lindsey et al. 2025, On the Biology of a Large Language Model)
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The attribution-graph formulation the paper adapts — nodes, edges, error nodes, and supernodes — is defined in these cited works.

concepts.name: J-lens attribution graphs
concepts.summary: Attribution graphs whose nodes are J-lens vectors selected by sparse decomposition at each layer and position, with remainder nodes for the non-J-space content — a verbalizable skeleton of the computation.
concepts.explanation: At each layer and position, sparse decomposition expresses the activation as a few J-lens vectors plus a non-J-space remainder; the selected vectors become named nodes and the remainder is collected into a remainder node. Edges are computed by backpropagating each node's coefficient one layer back with attention patterns and normalization denominators frozen; gradients flow through the MLP nonlinearity itself, unlike transcoder-based graphs. On the arithmetic prompt, the graph shows 21, 42, and 49 as named nodes in computation order, and reveals that the model fuses the operator and operand into a doubled operation, with coordinate swaps confirming the structure — replacing doubled with tripled flips the answer to 70, and swapping the same value into different intermediates produces different answers because different computation is applied downstream of each. The graphs are a partial account: most influence flows through remainder nodes, which is what the capacity results predict, since most computation runs outside the J-space — the first addition, for instance, is invisible, taking place entirely outside it. A second caveat is that the greedy pursuit can name a near-miss correlate of a concept still forming and land on the concept itself only layers later.

concepts.name: Supernode
concepts.summary: A graph node grouping J-lens vectors across adjacent layers and near-equivalent tokens — for example twent, 26, and 29 grouped under the 21 node.
concepts.explanation: Each displayed node in the paper's graphs is a supernode, in the sense of Ameisen et al.: it groups J-lens vectors across adjacent layers and across near-equivalent tokens, with the grouped contents listed under each node. Grouping absorbs the pursuit's near-misses — tokens like twent that stand in for a concept still sharpening across depth — into the node for the concept itself.

citedFrom.refText: Ameisen et al. (2025). Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models. Transformer Circuits
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The supernode grouping convention used in the paper's graphs is taken from this cited work.

concepts.name: Remainder node
concepts.summary: The node at each site collecting the non-J-space part of the activation, analogous to the error nodes of the original attribution-graph formulation.
concepts.explanation: The sparse decomposition at each layer and position leaves a residual that no J-lens vector accounts for; this is collected into a remainder node, analogous to the error nodes in the original attribution-graph formulation. Remainder nodes carry most of the influence on the output in the paper's graphs, and they are where invisible computation shows up: the literal 2 in the arithmetic prompt contributes only through the remainder at its token position, and the first addition flows entirely through remainders.

concepts.name: Interpreting components with the J-lens
concepts.summary: Projecting any weight direction — SAE features, transcoder encoders and decoders, attention-head weight matrices — through the J-lens to read what the component represents or transforms.
concepts.explanation: Any direction in residual-stream space can be projected through the J-lens just as an activation can, and when the resulting token distribution is sharply peaked, the top tokens often help interpret the component; comparing readouts across a component's input and output sides can reveal the transformation it implements. The paper's examples include an SAE feature whose activating contexts suggest "technical exposition" but whose lens readout — fake, fraud, suspicious — identifies it as a fabricated-content detector, confirmed by steering; transcoder translation features whose encoders read a multilingual concept plus French context and whose decoders write the French word's opening token; arithmetic transcoder features whose encoder and decoder readouts reveal the function computed, prompt-free; and an attention head whose four weight matrices, read through the lens, suggest it maps British spellings to Commonwealth nationalities. This gives a data-free complement to inspecting top activating contexts, which can mislead when a feature encodes an abstract assessment whose surface correlates are incidental.

concepts.name: Transcoders
concepts.summary: Sparsely activating approximations of a model's MLP layers, in which each feature has separate encoder and decoder directions.
concepts.explanation: Transcoders are trained to approximate a model's MLP layers with a sparsely activating hidden layer. Each feature has an encoder direction, which determines what residual-stream content activates it, and a decoder direction, which determines what it writes back. The separation of the two sides is what makes them useful under the J-lens: reading each side separately can reveal the input-to-output transformation the feature implements, as in the paper's translation and arithmetic examples.
